win_claim.quote: For problems where class-imbalance learning methods really help, both EasyEnsemble and BalanceCascade have higher AUC, F-measure, and G-mean than almost all other compared methods, and the former is superior than the latter.

uncertain: how_obtained original vs modified relies on whether each dataset is natively binary; paper only says 'Target is used as minority class, and all others are used as majority class' and does not print native class counts (Table II, p.4)
n_features left null: paper prints attribute composition (e.g. '1N,7C') not a total; totals not computed per schema (Table II, p.4)
Dataset printed 'satimage' in Table II but 'sat' in Tables IV/X; treated as same dataset (p.4, p.8)
best_other excludes Easy and SMOTE but includes BalanceCascade (co-proposed method); ties listed with '/' (Tables X, XI, p.8-9)
All result tables are images; values transcribed visually from 200/300 dpi renders (p.8-9)
notes: Paper proposes two methods: EasyEnsemble (Easy) and BalanceCascade (Cascade); Easy recorded as proposed per instruction, conclusion says Easy is superior to Cascade on 'hard' tasks. SMOTE baseline is SMOTE + AdaBoost (CART weak learners, 40 iterations, k=5; |P'|=|P| synthetic, majority subsampled to 2|P| when |N|>2|P|; SMOTE-NC for nominal attributes). Over and SMB not reported on 'easy' tasks due to training cost (footnote 3, p.6). AUC (Tables IV-V) and F-measure (Tables VII-VIII) also per-dataset; G-mean chosen per metric priority. Table XIII compares stacking vs original ensemble strategy (AUC). No supplementary material referenced.
